# Could Google's Next TPU Shift Back to TSMC? Inside the EMIB vs. CoWoS Battle

Source: https://substack..bHaGt0MrvTK5vKoOIfU6bHhJP7QqaWl1TlpgAH3dTCk?&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email

Amid the flood of headline-grabbing announcements at Computex last week, one development largely slipped under the radar.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang（黃仁勳） unveiled a humanoid robot reference platform developed in collaboration with China’s Unitree Robotics（宇樹科技）. The platform combines Unitree’s H2 humanoid robot—standing roughly 180 centimeters tall and weighing 68 kilograms—with Nvidia’s Blackwell-based Jetson Thor AI computer and dexterous robotic hands from Singapore-based Sharpa.
Five days later, at an international forum hosted by the Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology (DSET), Martijn Rasser, Senior Vice President for Technology and National Security at the U.S. think tank Special Competitive Studies Project (SCSP), openly questioned the move. He warned that Nvidia’s partnership could help make Chinese robots the global standard.
The remark caught me by surprise.
During a break in the conference, I approached Jason Fiorillo, Chief Legal Officer of Boston Dynamics, and asked whether that scenario was really plausible.
The American robotics pioneer—which once led the humanoid robotics industry but has since been overtaken in market share by the lower-cost Unitree—offered a more measured view. It is not that simple, Fiorillo said, because Nvidia’s partnership with Unitree is not exclusive.
Indeed, during his subsequent visit to South Korea, Huang also announced plans to deepen Nvidia’s robotics collaboration with Hyundai Motor Group, the parent company of Boston Dynamics.
Still, the episode highlights the growing concern among U.S. think tanks and academic circles over the latest developments within China’s supply chain ecosystem.
Chris Miller, author of
Chip War
（《晶片戰爭》）, made a similar point during an appearance on my podcast. He argued that the U.S.-Taiwan alliance should pay closer attention to preventing China from replicating in physical AI what it has achieved in electric vehicles: supply-chain dominance. That concern extends to emerging sectors such as robotics and drones.
Ironically, Nvidia’s partnership with Unitree sparked criticism inside China itself. Some online commentators accused Unitree of being unpatriotic for choosing Nvidia GPUs over Huawei alternatives.
Back to this week’s newsletter.
Last week marked the first time I heard Broadcom CEO Hock Tan（陳福陽） voluntarily mention MediaTek by name.
For executives at major technology companies, publicly commenting on competitors is rare.
The occasion was a Bloomberg interview. Tan noted that Broadcom’s key customer Google was working with a smaller partner on custom AI chips. He specifically named MediaTek and jokingly referred to the company as an “ankle-biter.”
The remark was clearly dismissive. But at the very least, it was also an acknowledgment that the bite hurts.
New details have continued to emerge around MediaTek’s second major AI ASIC engagement with Google—the ninth-generation TPU program.
Increasingly, evidence suggests the project may shift away from the equal partnership structure seen in the eighth-generation TPU, with MediaTek’s co-developed version emerging as Google’s primary path, while Broadcom’s design increasingly serves as a contingency option.
The project is one of the most closely watched chip programs in the industry, with implications for the future competitive balance among Google, Nvidia, Anthropic, and other AI heavyweights.
One critical question remains:
Will Intel’s EMIB-T advanced packaging technology—the 2.5D packaging platform Google has boldly chosen for the project—prove capable of delivering at scale, or will it become the program’s Achilles’ heel?
That is the focus of this week’s newsletter.
